content: Active surveillance has demonstrated higher rates of early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) detection and improved three-year survival rates. While the role of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in HCC screening has been debated, recent guidelines recommend combining ultrasound with AFP testing, as this combination achieves a sensitivity of 63% for detecting early-stage HCC. Additional blood-based biomarkers, such as DNA methylation-based assays (e.g., OncoGuard Liver), proteomic, glycomic (e.g., GlycoTest), and metabolomic biomarkers, as well as combination assays, are under active development and may enhance HCC screening. The most significant risk factors for developing HCC include the presence of cirrhosis, HBeAg positivity, persistently high HBV DNA levels, a family history of HCC, age over 40 years (reflecting prolonged infection and accumulated liver damage), elevated ALT levels (>45 U/L), and co-infection with HIV or HCV. Ethnicity also plays a role, with individuals of African or Asian descent being at higher risk. Other contributing factors include neonatal or childhood HBV infection, specific HBV genotypes (e.g., C, A1, F), core promoter mutations, aflatoxin exposure, HDV co-infection, smoking, high alcohol intake, and diabetes. Risk calculators have been developed to predict HCC risk in individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) using clinical and laboratory data, such as age, sex, albumin, bilirubin, ALT levels, HBeAg status, HBV DNA levels, and cirrhosis presence. These models stratify individuals into low, intermediate, or high-risk categories. Examples include the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer staging system and the GAG-HCC risk score. Recent advancements incorporate transient elastography as a substitute for HBV DNA levels, improving the performance of models like LSM-HCC and mREACH-B. Emerging evidence suggests that HBcrAg, a surrogate for cccDNA concentrations, may also aid in HCC risk assessment. Routine HCC surveillance, typically involving ultrasound and AFP testing every six months, is recommended for high-risk individuals with CHB, particularly those with cirrhosis or a family history of HCC. Surveillance aims to detect HCC at earlier stages, enabling curative treatment and improving survival. However, potential harms include false-positive results, unnecessary interventions, and increased costs. The effectiveness of surveillance depends on the availability of treatment options for small HCCs, such as ablation, resection, or antiviral therapy, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Antiviral therapy plays a critical role in reducing HCC risk and improving outcomes, even among individuals with HCC. Lifelong nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy is recommended for individuals with cirrhosis to prevent HBV reactivation and associated complications. Discontinuation of therapy may be considered in select cases, such as those achieving HBeAg seroconversion and sustained undetectable HBV DNA levels, but requires careful monitoring for reactivation. Relapse is common after stopping therapy, and retreatment is recommended if reactivation occurs. The primary goals of antiviral therapy in CHB are to prevent progression to severe liver disease, HCC, and death by suppressing HBV DNA to undetectable levels. While nucleos(t)ide analogues are effective in inhibiting HBV replication, they do not eliminate cccDNA or integrated viral genomes, necessitating long-term therapy for most individuals. Finite treatment may be possible for select individuals achieving specific virological milestones, but this remains uncommon.
